html:
The map's label for the canoe peoples of the fjords and islands of southern Chile and Tierra del Fuego, shown from 1500 BCE to 1815. The best known are the Yaghan (Yámana) around Cape Horn and the Kawésqar (Alacaluf) further north, with the Chono beyond them.

The land is cold, wet and windy, with no farming. Families lived much of the time in bark canoes, keeping a small fire burning on a clay hearth in the boat. Women paddled and dived for shellfish in icy water; men hunted sea lions and seals with harpoons; a stranded whale meant a feast for many families. They wore little clothing and kept warm with fire and seal grease. Their shell middens line the coasts.

On land their neighbours were different peoples: the Selk'nam, who hunted guanaco on the main island of Tierra del Fuego, and the Tehuelche of the Patagonian steppe.

Europeans arrived in 1520, when Ferdinand Magellan sailed through the strait now named after him and called the land Tierra del Fuego for the fires he saw on shore. In 1832 and 1833 Charles Darwin met Yaghan people on the voyage of the Beagle and wrote of them harshly. In the 1800s sealers, missionaries, settlers and disease brought a collapse of these peoples. Small Yaghan and Kawésqar communities remain today.
